title: KV cache fragment-aware binning and fast-path eviction playbook
content:
Status: in_review

Summary:
This doc proposes a pragmatic, low-latency KV cache allocation and eviction playbook that focuses on reducing fragmentation while preserving SLOs for tail-latency. Goals are: (1) keep hot-key lookup+update on a fast path with no locking, (2) avoid long pauses from large compaction jobs, (3) bound memory amplification from fragmentation, and (4) provide clear telemetry and knobs for ops.

Context & motivation:
- We see rising memory amplification on long-lived processes when workload mixes many small transient entries with a small number of very large cached tensors. Current slabless allocator + generic free lists lead to high external fragmentation and unpredictable compaction costs.
- Past proposals focused on large-scale compaction (background rewrite) or big monolithic slabs; both have tradeoffs we want to avoid for hosted low-latency inference.

Non-goals:
- Replace the existing KV store wire-format. This is allocator/eviction/compaction only.
- Solve application-level cache sharding (that is complementary).

Design principles:
- Fragment-awareness over fixed-size-only slabs: size-class binning should consider both entry size distribution and fragmentation created when entries die.
- Fast-path reads/writes: per-core/Shard small-lock or lock-free structure for hot lookups.
- Cooperative background compaction: bounded, interruptible, and incremental.
- NUMA-conscious allocation: allocate close to the accessing CPU where possible.
- Observability-first: expose fragmentation ratio, free-runway (ms), compaction backlog, eviction-induced tail-latency.

High-level design (components):
1) Fragment-aware binning allocator (FAB):
   - Bins are not just by request size; each bin has a fragmentation budget counter and an aging window.
   - Two orthogonal axes: nominal size-class (power-of-two-ish buckets) and frag-score (low/medium/high). Frag-score is a small integer derived from historical reclaim inefficiency for that bucket.
   - Allocation flow: lookup hot-path bin (per-shard) -> attempt allocation from local freelist -> if miss, probe sibling bins with small growth factor -> if still miss, fall back to global pool (which can trigger preemptive compaction).

2) Slotted micro-pools for tiny entries (<= 512 bytes):
   - Fixed slot arrays that keep entries packed; on eviction we return slots to free bitmaps. Small-entry operations remain lockless using atomic bitmaps per core.
   - Purpose: avoid small-entry churn causing holes in larger pools.

3) Size-weighted fast-path eviction (SWFE):
   - Fast path: for small-to-medium bins, eviction uses a ring-queue of candidate keys with approximate recency (tiny per-bucket LRU hints). Eviction cost is O(1) typical.
   - Weighting: each candidate has a size weight; eviction chooses by weighted benefit (evicting one large entry may free space for many small entries).

4) Generational compaction & background rewriter:
   - Entries are tagged with a generation id on allocate. The background compactor prefers reclaiming high-generation (cold) regions first and will attempt to pack surviving entries into contiguous new regions to reduce fragmentation.
   - Compaction is incremental: rewrite tasks are scheduled with a token bucket (max bytes/sec) and interruptible on latency pressure.

5) NUMA and kernel hints:
   - Per-node pools and allocation affinity. On cross-node misses, prefer migrating smaller entries versus allocating new large regions across nodes.
   - Use madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) and madvise(MADV_FREE) where available for rapid OS-side reclaim of freed pages in compacted regions. Consider mlock only for pinned hot slabs.

6) Fast fallback policy for capacity pressure:
   - If free-runway (ms of requestable allocs before hitting high watermark) < threshold, trigger aggressive tiny-entry eviction and raise compaction throttle temporarily. This is an ops-configurable policy.

Telemetry and observability:
- Fragmentation ratio = live_bytes / (allocated_region_bytes - free_holes_bytes). Emit per-bin and global.
- Free runway = estimated requests/ms until watermark.
- Compaction backlog = bytes queued for rewrite.
- Eviction impact events: when eviction latency > 95th SLO, mark event and include candidate sizes and source bin.
- Export histograms: per-op allocation latency, per-eviction latency, compaction chunk latency.

Interplay with scheduler and kernels:
- Short allocations (tiny/slotted) are always satisfied on the local core; they avoid scheduler preemption where possible.
- Compaction tasks run on a dedicated pool of background threads; they expose low-priority cgroups/nice levels and are preemptible by serving threads.
- Kernel-level optimizations: prefer hugetlb for very large regions to reduce TLB pressure; use madvise hints during compaction to let kernel asynchronously reclaim freed pages.

Eviction heuristics (detailed):
- Candidate selection: combine approximate LRU score (decayed counters), size weight, and frag-score of the bin (prefer reclaim in bins with high frag-score).
- Eviction scoring function (pseudo):
  score = (recency_decay / (1 + size_kb)) * frag_multiplier
  pick candidate with lowest score but prioritize actions that reduce fragmentation metric (e.g., reclaiming a large, isolated chunk).
- For heavy write workloads, favor write-back eviction (defer physical free) to batch frees for compaction jobs.

Backpressure and safety nets:
- Soft/Hard watermarks: on soft, begin aggressive eviction and lower compaction token bucket; on hard, reject non-essential allocations and return OOM-ish error to caller with telemetry tag.
- EvictionSAFE flag: allow callers to mark entries as non-evictable briefly (e.g., when pinned in an inference pipeline). The allocator tracks pinned counts to avoid reclaiming in-use data.

Testing & validation plan:
- Microbenchmarks: allocation latency for sizes {64B,512B,4KB,128KB,1MB}, eviction latency distribution under synthetic churn.
- Long-run soak: run 7-day mixed workload (many small tensors + periodic large model sharded entries) and measure fragmentation ratio and compaction traffic.
- Chaos tests: pause background compactor threads, simulate high NUMA-cross traffic, verify graceful fallback.
- A/B production rollout: 10% canary -> 30% -> 100% with per-canary telemetry checks (fragmentation delta, tail-latency changes).

Telemetry thresholds for rollback:
- fragmentation ratio increase > 12% vs baseline OR
- 95th allocation latency regression > 2x OR
- compaction IO spike > 3x baseline for > 10m

Operational knobs (configurable at runtime):
- bin_growth_factor: how aggressively to try sibling bins
- compaction_tokens_per_sec: bytes/sec budget
- fast_eviction_threshold: free-runway(ms) cutoff
- slotted_pool_slot_size and limits per-shard
- numa_migration_enabled (bool)

Open questions / tradeoffs:
1) How many frag-score buckets are useful in practice? Start with 3 (low/med/high) and iterate.
2) Should compaction be led by memory pressure signals only or also by periodic maintenance windows? (ops input needed)
3) Degree of per-core state: more per-core state reduces contention but increases meta-memory and complexity for compaction.
4) Hardware offload: can we use RDMA or shared-P2P GPU memory primitives to avoid host-side compaction for some workloads? (long-term)

Implementation notes and rough timeline (Q4):
- Week 0-2: implement slotted micro-pool and per-shard freelist API + unit tests.
- Week 3-5: FAB allocator with frag-score bookkeeping + local tests.
- Week 6-8: background compactor incremental rewrite, compaction token bucket, integration tests.
- Week 9-10: canary rollout, telemetry dashboards, iterate.

Appendix: short pseudo-flow for allocation:
- alloc(size):
  1) if size <= slot_max: try slotted micro-pool (lockless fast-path)
  2) else: look up local bin -> try freelist pop -> if miss probe sibling bins within growth_factor -> if still miss request from global pool (may schedule compaction)
  3) if global pool exhausted: trigger fast-path eviction (SWFE) and retry -> if still fails return allocation error

End of doc.
